content.title: About
content.content: Oysters are marine bivalve mollusks that live in coastal waters of seas and oceans. Their flesh is tender, mildly sweet, and carries a distinct briny flavor. Oysters are commonly served baked in the oven or quickly broiled on a grill, often with butter, garlic, or herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One gram of oysters can filter up to 50 liters of water per day, helping to clean their environment.
Oysters are considered an aphrodisiac because of their high zinc content.
Ancient cultures used oysters as a remedy for wounds and skin conditions.
There are over 100 oyster species, but the Pearl, Kokanee, and Pacific oysters are most popular in cuisine.
Oysters can change sex several times during their life, starting as males and later becoming females.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Zinc supports the immune system, aids wound healing, and plays a role in reproductive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and proper nervous system function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Oysters are low in calories yet provide high‑quality protein and valuable micronutrients.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and reduce inflammatory processes.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron is necessary for oxygen transport in the blood and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw or undercooked oysters may contain Vibrio bacteria, which can cause gastroenteritis.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oysters, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Oysters naturally contain a fair amount of sodium; people monitoring salt intake should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy metal accumulation
items.content: In certain regions oysters can accumulate cadmium or lead, so it is important to source them from reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake oysters in the oven with butter, garlic, and herbs for 5‑7 minutes at 200 °C, or quickly broil them until the edges turn lightly golden. Serve with lemon wedges, tartar sauce, or a simple soy sauce. Rinse oysters thoroughly under cold water before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live oysters in the refrigerator on a tray covered with a damp cloth, no more than 24 hours. Cooked oysters should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Discard any oysters with shells that do not close when tapped gently.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned lentil soup with reduced sodium is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected red or green lentils, vegetables, and spices. The lower salt level makes it suitable for people monitoring their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the oldest legumes, cultivated for over 8,000 years.
Canning preserves nutrients and flavor without the need for refrigeration.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with herbs and spices such as thyme and bay leaf.
Lentil soup is often used in weight‑loss diets because of its high protein and fiber content.
In many cultures, lentil soup is a traditional dish during fasting periods.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Lentils provide about 9 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes gut health.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps control blood pressure and reduces strain on the cardiovascular system.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron supports oxygen transport, while folate is essential for DNA synthesis and pregnancy health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in lentils combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Preservative content
items.content: Although sodium is reduced, canned products may contain additives that some people are sensitive to.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Certain varieties may contain a small amount of added sugar; check the label if you monitor sugar intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the soup in the microwave or on the stove until boiling, optionally add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a drizzle of olive oil to enhance flavor. Serve with whole‑grain bread or crackers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer any leftovers to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
